notes.meaning: Many tax collectors and known sinners came close to listen to Jesus speak. Tax collectors were despised by other Jews because they worked for the Roman rulers and often cheated people. Jesus welcomed these outcasts instead of pushing them away.

The Pharisees and religious teachers began to grumble against Jesus. In Jewish culture, sharing a meal was a sign of close friendship and acceptance, so eating with open sinners shocked them. Jesus spent time with sinners not to join in their wrongs, but to offer them spiritual healing.

Jesus replied to the complaints of the religious leaders by telling them a set of stories called parables. A parable is an earthly story that teaches a heavenly truth. He used these stories to show what God's heart is truly like toward the lost.

Jesus asked His hearers to picture a shepherd who owns one hundred sheep and loses just one. A caring shepherd leaves the ninety-nine safely grazing in the pasture to search for the missing one until he finds it. In the same way, God actively searches for each person who strays away from Him.

When the shepherd finds the tired, lost sheep, he does not beat it or scold it. Instead, he gladly lifts it onto his own shoulders and carries it. This picture shows how gently the Savior carries weak and helpless sinners back to safety.

After carrying the sheep home, the shepherd invites his friends and neighbors to celebrate with him. Finding what was lost brings a joy that is too big to keep to oneself. God wants others to share in His happiness when a lost soul is recovered.

Jesus explained that heaven bursts with joy over even one sinner who repents. To repent means to change your mind and turn away from sin to follow God. Heaven rejoices far more over a saved sinner than over people who proudly think they are already good enough and need no help.

Jesus offered a second picture of a woman who owned ten silver coins and lost one in her house. Homes back then were dark with dirt floors, so she had to light an oil lamp and sweep carefully to find it. God searches for lost people with that same focused and patient effort.

When the woman finally spots the lost coin, she calls her friends and neighbors together to celebrate. The relief of finding her treasure makes her want everyone around her to be glad. The story shows how natural it is to celebrate when valuable things are recovered.

Jesus told His listeners that God and His angels rejoice whenever a single sinner turns back to God. God does not take pleasure in seeing people destroyed by their sins. He delights with pure joy when someone is restored to His family.

Jesus then told a third story about a father who had two sons. This parable explains God's love even more deeply by showing how a father deals with two very different boys. The younger son represents open sinners, while the older son represents religious leaders who are cold at heart.

The younger son asked his father to give him his share of the family property right away. Asking for an inheritance early was like telling the father that he wished he were already dead. Even so, the father granted the request and divided his estate between both sons.

A short time later, the younger son turned his share into cash and traveled to a distant foreign land. There he threw away all his wealth on reckless and wild living. Leaving the father's house led him straight into foolish choices and spiritual ruin.

Just as the son ran out of money, a terrible famine spread across that whole region. He suddenly found himself starving and alone, without anything left to buy food. Sin promises total freedom, but it always leaves a person empty and in desperate need.

To stay alive, the young man hired himself out to a local citizen who sent him into the fields to feed pigs. For a Jewish person, pigs were unclean animals that God had forbidden them to touch or eat. Doing this job meant the young man had sunk to the lowest shame imaginable.

The young man was so hungry that he wished he could eat the dry bean pods meant for the pigs. Not a single person in that foreign country gave him anything to eat. When hard times came, all his so-called friends disappeared and left him to starve.

At last, the young man came to his senses and realized how blind he had been. He remembered that even the day-laborers in his father's house had plenty of bread, while he was dying of hunger. True repentance begins when someone honestly faces their own misery and remembers how good God is.

The son made up his mind to stand up, travel home, and speak to his father. He planned to confess that he had sinned both against God in heaven and against his father on earth. He knew he had no excuses left to offer.

The son decided to admit that he had lost all right to be called a son. He planned to ask his father to hire him as a common day-laborer just so he could survive. Real repentance does not make demands, but comes with a humble heart ready to take the lowest place.

The young man got up and began the long journey back to his father. While he was still a long way off, his father saw him, felt deep compassion, and ran to throw his arms around him and kiss him. In that culture, older men did not run, but the father cared only about welcoming his lost child.

The son began his prepared speech, confessing that he had sinned against heaven and his father and was no longer worthy to be a son. His father's warm kiss did not stop his confession, but made him even more aware of his guilt. God meets our honest confessions with deep grace and forgiveness.

Before the son could ask to be a servant, the father commanded the staff to bring out the finest robe, a signet ring, and sandals. The fine robe honored him, the ring restored his family authority, and shoes showed he was a free son rather than a barefoot slave. God does not treat returning sinners like second-class servants, but restores them fully.

The father told the servants to prepare the fattened calf, an animal saved for the most special celebrations. He wanted the whole household to feast, sing, and be glad. God welcomes returning sinners with overflowing celebration rather than grudging tolerance.

The father announced that this celebration was necessary because his son had been as good as dead, but was now alive again. Being cut off from the father's love was like death, but turning home brought new life. With that, the grand feast began.

While the party was going on inside, the older son was out working hard in the fields. As he walked toward the house at the end of the day, he heard music and dancing. He was surprised to find a large celebration happening without his knowledge.

The older brother called over one of the household servants to find out what was happening. Instead of going inside to check on his family, he stayed outside and asked questions. His distance showed that his heart was already separated from his father's joy.

The servant told him that his younger brother had come home safe and in good health. Because the boy had returned unharmed, the father had killed the fattened calf to celebrate. The servant shared the family's joy, expecting the older brother to be happy too.

Instead of rejoicing, the older brother became angry and refused to step foot inside the house. His father came outside and gently urged him to come in. This shows how patiently God deals even with proud, bitter people who resent His mercy to others.

The older brother complained that he had slaved for years and obeyed every order, yet never received even a young goat to party with his friends. He viewed his life at home as hard labor that deserved payment rather than as a loving relationship. A self-righteous attitude turns obedience into bitter slavery.

The older brother bitterly pointed out that the younger son had wasted the family fortune on shameful living, yet received the prize calf the moment he arrived. He would not even call him his brother, calling him 'this son of yours' instead. Bitterness and jealousy make people cruel toward others and blind to the beauty of mercy.

The father answered tenderly, reminding the older son that he had always been with him and that the whole estate was his to enjoy. The older brother had never needed to earn his father's favor or wait for permission to enjoy what was already his. God's lavish grace toward new believers takes nothing away from those who have walked with Him for years.

The father insisted that they had to celebrate, because this young man was the older boy's own brother who had been dead and was now alive. Jesus left the story without an ending, challenging the Pharisees to choose whether they would enter God's joy or stay outside in their pride. God calls all His people to rejoice whenever a lost sinner is brought home.
